Charleston, S. C., June 8, 1903. To His Excellency Gov. Heyward, Columbia, S. C.

Sir: I most respectfully appeal to you for the protection of my life and property in the town of Eutawville, S. C., by our good office.

Since the sad killing of my brother, John A. Fludd by citizens of said town my life and property have been and are still in danger.

To get me away from my house, sets of prosecutions without causes were charged against me in the State courts first, and then in the United States courts and again in the magistrate courts in Berkeley and Clarendon counties with no protection for my own property.

Seeing this was too shameful, I was held for carrying concealed weapons in Clarendon county before Justice Richbourg. This is something that everybody knows me not to be guilty of.

Now I rented a store and house for one year to one of those that were charged with the killing of Fludd. I did not break my contract with said party on account of this occurrence, and since the lease was out, January, this man was backed up by the town and community of Eutawville, S. C., to hold my property by force and refuse to pay rent for two months in last year and for all of this year.

I place the matter in the magistrate court for collection and on my return from taking testimonies in my congressional contest and those who were witnesses for Mr. Geo. S. Lagree in this county.

About the first of April last on the 8th of the same month, I was forced to leave my home to save myself from being lynched after a pretended arrest, and have not been able to go home since.

My property is being taken by force and used and I am threatened to be shot down if I be seen in Entawville, S. C., and I have no redress.

My white and colored friends have advised me to leave the county but I am resisting the same because my property and interest are in that county. I am a law-abiding citizen and the county, regardless of color know this to be a fact, that it is nothing but a conspiracy and prejudice against me.

I place the matter before you for your good judgment in the premises as governor of the whole people, white, colored, rich and poor.

I am, most respectfully,

Aaron P. Prioleau.

No. 470 King street,

aaron-p-prioleau-eutawville-1903-04.A4:
GOVERNER WRITES TO PRIOLEAU.
The Colored Aspirant for Congress Who Claims That He is Banished From His Home.
Aaron Prioleau's letter has been answered by Gov. Heyward. But the colored Republican who is contesting Mr. Geo. S. Legare's election to congress gets little satisfaction out of that letter. Prioleau complained that on account of his eminence as a candidate he is subject to persecution and has been run out of his home town, Eutawville. He of course presented one side of the question and the reply of the governor, while dignified and kindly in tone, shows Prioleau that he can get redress in the courts if he has a grievance. The governor says in his letter: "From your letter I gather that you complain that the magistrate courts, the State court and the United States courts have been used as a means of persecution and that you can not obtain justice in those tribunals. Of course I feel it unnecessary to say that as to the United States tribunals the State authorities have no control over its operations. If the magistrate courts have been used unjustly I suggest that you refer the same to the grand jury of the county and the presiding Judge and I am satisfied that upon the complaint such action will be taken as will give you a fair trial. Then, too, if you have been held under charges that were groundless and the action of the officers was malicious you have a cause of action for an action for malicious prosecution. You do not state in your communication that you have resorted to this remedy and I suggest that if there is a case of malicious persecution that you appeal to the courts.

"As to your suggestion that the contract for the rent of a store was violated I beg to suggest that the proper tribunal for redress is that of a civil action in the courts and if a local magistrate will not give justice you have the right, upon the proper affidavit, to have the case transferred. I regret to note the suggestion that you are compelled to remain from home on account of threats and I am satisfied that if you apply to the local civil authorities such action will be taken as to protect your rights as a citizen. And I suggest further that you send to this office evidence of the fact that the local officers have declined to give you such protection as the law guaranatees, and I will then take the matter up with the view to seeing that you are given legal protection.

"The only record that I have before me is your communication, and the facts are too meagre for me to take any executive action, and as above suggested please send me your charges in some tangible form in order that I may give it consideration.
"You may rest assured that as chief executive I will do all in my power to see that you have all the civil rights and privileges of a citizen of this State."

Illinois, the land of Abraham Lincoln, is giving the "uncivilized South" a few lessons in the race problem. A colored school teacher fatally wounded a white man in a dispute about some school matters. It soon brought an angry mob together, and while the wounded man was still living, and for aught they knew would recover, they swung the colored teacher up by a rope and tortured him nearly to death, and then saturated his body with coal oil and set it on fire. We have heard of no such atrocious act as this in the South for such a provocation. The last act of the mob is an order issued that all colored people must leave that part of the State under the penalty of death. So we see the Northern friends of the colored people are not much friends after all.

A colored man was killed in Indianapolis Wednesday by a mob of two hundred people because they thought he made an insulting remark to a thirteen-year-old white girl he met on the street. In no place in the South, which they have villified and abused so much, would such a supposition form a pretext to take human life. It looks as if the horrors of the race prejudice are taking place principally in the North, even in those States that are generally found in the Republican column. The authorities at Johnson City, Tennessee, rescued a colored man from a mob on last Thursday after he had been hung up, and saved his life. He had brutally assaulted a white woman, who it is thought will die. How different was the action of the Tennessee authorities to that of the authorities of the States of Illinois and Indiana.—Free Lance.

A new pattern woven of the old strands, a new variation of the universal and eternal theme, a new play with the old, old motive—a new story of a man and a woman and the interlocking of their hearts forms the subject of "The Silver Poppy," by Arthur Stringer. It is a unique rendition, a version fresh with the perennial freshness of human passion, with an individuality to distinguish it from the infinitude of other versions.

One has not gone far with the story of John Hartley and his alluring Cordelia before reaching the verdict that it is an artful piece of fiction with subtle power, and the verdict is not weakened, but gradually and surely confirmed to the end. It is a sudden, solemnous spell which the author casts over the reader, and, once exerted, it is clinging and lasting. When John, the starving novice in letters, meets Cordelia, the newly celebrated novelist, at a studio gathering the touch of their hands awakes the reader's interest as with a spark; there is a suggestion of unusualness amid commonplaces, and this suggestion is ever present throughout the tale's development.

Cordelia Vaughn, a rare blend of deceit and sincerity, selfishness and self-sacrifice, of impulsiveness and cold deliberation, securely captures the reader's affections, beguiling him into a confidence which he is loath to surrender. Indeed, it is doubtful whether the average man will bring himself eventually to distrust and despise her. In all apparent honesty she sets her heart upon John Hartley—had she a purpose at the very outset? The question is difficult to answer, even when the whole story is known at the end. But, whether or no she sought his heart because she wished to make him her tool, certain it is that she made fair return of love; she gave him her own freely. The woman loved from the beginning, always, undeviatingly—with this reflection the reader may attempt to excuse his own overweening lenency toward her—love covers a multitude of the reader's sins.

She was ingenuous, she was intensely human in her frailty, and at times it was her very love for John that inspired her fraud upon him—he had the grace to give her full motives for that, even when he divined her under-motives and deceptions. If, as is sometimes asserted, the purpose of a novel is merely to tempt the fancy with a woman, Mr. Stringer has achieved conspicuous success.

ZINC ORE PRICES FIRM; SUPPLY CUT TO DEMAND. Effort to Bear the Market Falls-Lead Ore Declines From Quota-tions of Last Week.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

Joplin, Mo., May 3.—The reserve stock of zinc ore, which was about 9,000 tons the first of February, has been purchased and shipped until there is estimated to be less than 1,000 tons of unsold ore remaining in the bins of the producers throughout the district at the present time.

An effort, started a few weeks ago, by some of the smelters to reduce the price is not meeting with success. Producers of high-grade ore decline to sell at a price reduction, and the result has been slow sales the fore part of each week, with brisk trade later.

The reserve stock is too low to permit an attempt to force the price down, when it is known that other smelters are ready and willing to step in and pay current prices should some try to lower it. The fact of the situation seems to be that several of the smelters have been holding back on their purchases hoping to get in on a lower price, until the stock at their smelting works has been reduced to a point where they must secure ore.

For instance the Cherokee-Lanyon Spelter Company, which has been out of the Joplin market since last fall, during which time Western ore has been treated, has resumed buying, and has found it necessary to advance prices on some bins to secure any ore at all.

It is rumored that this company paid the highest price of the week, $41.50 per ton, in order to secure a particularly desirable bin of ore.

Other bins of high-grade ore sold at $11 per ton, and while this ore was sold on straight bids, it is equivalent to a basis of $5 per ton for 60 per cent zinc. Ore assaying below 60 per cent and above 58 per cent zinc sold on an assay basis of $37 per ton and ore of lower grade sold on a $36 and $35 basis, there being a change of $1 per ton for each two points of assay.

There was marketed the past week 5,107 tons of zinc ore, very close to if not the actual output for the week. The small stock on hand makes lower prices impracticable at this time, and there is little likelihood that prices will be soon reduced, at least while the demand is so near equal to the output.

Lead ore sold during the week at $54.50 per ton, a decline in the price from $59.50 the previous week. The lead smelters are still paying a proportionately higher price, based on the pig lead quotations, than was paid under the old system of buying in vogue here for many years. At the present price of pig lead and of ore the margin of profit for smelting is very close.

VICKSBURG, Miss., May 4.—Tom Morris and Ben Bryant, negroes, who were arrested Saturday for the murder of William Legg, a planter, at Adam's Landing, and who confessed, were lynched before daylight yesterday morning by a mob composed of the "best citizens" in that part of the country. ROPE BROKE AND NEGRO, HANGED BY MOB, ESCAPED. Tom Morris Dropped Into Water From Bridge Over Yasoo River and Eluded Pursuers.
Vicksburg, Miss., May 4.—Tom Morris, the negro murderer of Mr. Herbert William Legg, who was hanged from a bridge on the Yazoo River Sunday with his accomplice, Ben Bryant, still lives.

Morris was believed to be dead when the mob departed.

The fact that he escaped his punishment came to light this afternoon, when a party of gentlemen went to the place of the hanging and found that the rope with which Morris had been hanged had evidently broken when he was shoved from the bridge, and falling into the shallow water in the creek below. Morris was enabled to get away after the mob dispersed.

His shoes and socks were left on the side of the creek and footprints led only a few yards, after which no trace of the murderer could be found. The news that Morris had escaped spread rapidly over the county and a determined posse is now scouring the woods for the murderer.

Mossi was the confessed murderer of Mr. Legg, the prominent planter whose gin was first fired Friday night and who was shot down in cold blood when he went back from the fire to his store, while Bryant, the other negro, who was successfully executed, was an accomplice in the crimes of firing the gin and then robbling Mr. Legg's store.

Nothing can be learned from Redwood at this hour concerning whether Morris has been recaptured.

bob-bryant-haynes-bluff-1903-05-02.A22:
MORE MOB VIOLENCE
Lynch law continues to assert itself. On Saturday, four persons were put to death by mobs. In Pemiscot County, Mo., a preacher and a constable were shot. The preacher had been arrested on the charge of living unlawfully with a woman who belonged to his "sect" and was also a preacher. The constable took his prisoner home with him for the night intending to take him to the county seat on the following day and lodge him in jail. At midnight a mob went to the constable's house, and when the constable opened the door in response to a knock, shot him. The preacher was then seized, dragged into the woods and shot. In this instance the victims of the mob were white persons.

A few hours later at Haynes Bluff, near Vicksburg, Miss., two negroes were lynched by a large mob of farmers, despite the protestations of officers. One of the negroes confessed, and in his confession implicated another negro. That was enough to satisfy the scruples of the mob, if it had any. Both men were hanged, and their bodies were left dangling from trees.

In neither instance was there the slightest excuse for lynching. In each case authorities were proceeding to administer legal punishment. Back of these fresh disgraces there was doubtless the same abnormal craving for excitement that has been so often commented on in relation to the violence of mobs. The shooting of the constable the custodian of a man under arrest, shows how little regard the mob had for anyone or anything. It is not stated that there was any grievance against the constable. The prisoner could have been taken from the constable, but it was more convenient to kill both men. The night's thrilling adventures were doubled by claiming two victims instead of one.

Several days ago a story was hatched out to the effect that two negroes were lynched at Hynes' Bluff in this state, that is the formality was gone through. Ropes were tied around their necks and the negroes shoved off a bridge sixty feet high. One rope broke and the nergo went sailing to the bottom of the cold stream of water below. The report continues to the effect that the negro was not killed by the fall, nor was he drowned, but picking up himself he hied away to other parts and is now enjoying life, liberty and the fond pursuit of a crap game.

A week or so before this occurrence a report comes from Alabama to the effect that a negro was legally hanged or supposed to have been hanged until he was dead and his soul had entered the kingdom of heaven. But it seems that his people, to whom his body was given for burial, discovered life in him and after a few hours' work brought him around all right and he is now gone to help the other negro shoot craps.

Some time ago near Drew in Sunflower county, this state, a negro was arrested on the charge of criminal assault on a white woman. The sheriff who had him in charge carrying him to jail was overpowered by a mob and the nergo was taken from him. He was carried off the road a short distance and the thirty men who composed the mob shot him thirty times. He was left for dead, being riddled with bullets, but the sheriff, who went to look after his burial, found that the nergo was still alive and within the next few weeks he was able to sit up. Soon thereafter he was tried and, being convicted and sentenced to the penitentiary, is now working on one of the convict farms. These three incidents go to show the recuperative powers of some negroes or they are the strongest kind of evidences of the recuperative powers of some correspondents to lie. A RACE RIOT WAS IMMINENT.

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

BRISTOL, VA., Aug. 24.—What came near resulting in a race riot happened on State Street, this city, Saturday afternoon. A burley, insolent negro man pushed a lady off the sidewalk. The incident was witnessed by several white men, and one took the lady's part, having made at the negro and struck him. The negro showed flight, and another dangerous-looking negro, who stood near, came to the assistance of the negro who had committed the offense. The negroes drew knives, and when the white man started across the street to arm himself, the negroes followed him with open knives. By this time a considerable crowd had gathered, and there were cries of "shoot," "lynch."

The negroes were quickly hustled away to prevent violence.

Negro Offered Whiskey Instead of Fare Cut Them With Razor, It Is Charged.
After offering a drink of whiskey in lieu of fare to Charles Manley, conductor of a Bath Beach motor train on its way from Coney Island at an early hour yesterday morning, Calvin R. Ferguson, a negro, drew a razor and, the police say, slashed the conductor and cut the guard, and after terrifying the carload of passengers jumped from the rapidly moving train.

The negro got on the train at Ulmer Park, holding a flask in his hand, according to the police. When Manley, the conductor, asked for his fare the negro produced no money, but offered him a drink of whiskey. This happened several times. Then the conductor tried to put the man off. Ferguson drew a razor, it is declared, and slashed Manley's hands and face. George Bender, the guard, who came to Manley's assistance, was also cut on the hands and arms. Then the negro ran through the car brandishing his razor. Several men who had started to stop him ducked in a hurry.

Jumping from the platform of the train into the marsh grass, Ferguson escaped. The train was stopped and a posse of men started back after the fugitive. Word was also sent to the Bath Beach police station, and the reserves were started out. They found Ferguson hiding in the meadows between Bath Beach and Bensonhurst. He emptied a revolver at his pursuers before he was captured. Manley and Bender had their wounds dressed by an ambulance surgeon and then went home. Ferguson was locked up on a charge of felonious assault, and will be arraigned to-morrow.

ELEVEN WHITECAPPERS HELD BY SHERIFF.
Alleged Slayers Of Detective Brown Under Arrest At Wynne-Coroner Continues Investigation Of Crime.
Wynne, Ark., March 13.—Considerable excitement prevails on the streets of Wynne over the exposure of the gang of whitecaps, an organized band of desperadoes know as the "Smith's Chapel Club." Eleven men are under close guard charged with being members of the gang and implicated in the assassination of Detective John H. Brown in the battle last Monday night which occurred within four miles of this city.

Twelve men impaneled as a coroner's jury have been in secret session for two days and are likely to continue in their deliberations the remainder of the week before a verdict is announced.

REIGN OF TERROR.

For two weeks the neighborhood southwest of Wynne has been in the throes of a reign of terror provoked by the midnight depredations of a band of lawless men who have been firing volleys of buckshot into the homes of both white and black and scaring the denizens out of their senses. According to the best information obtainable, the recent rioting is an outburst from a religious difference that began last fall in a Baptist and Methodist settlement by a protracted meeting inaugurated by the Christian church, or Campbellites. The neighborhood four miles southwest of Wynne is largely composed of Methodists and Baptists. A Campbellite minister intruded in their midst and began a revival. As a result a Christian church was promulgated and a house of worship built by the denomination. Among its membership was R. R. Fallis, a wealthy planter. A few weeks later it was burned to the ground. There was never sufficient evidence gathered to convict any one and apparently the matter dropped.

WHITE RENTERS OUSTED.

When the time arrived for the renewal of contracts between the land owners and the renters for the crop of 1903 the negroes were the successful bidders, and the white renters became without jobs. Soon after, the organized band sprung into active existence and rioting began in earnest. On trees and upon houses warnings were posted a la the ancient ku klxu plan, and negroes were warned to rid the county of their presence or take the consequences. A mounted band rode through the neighborhood at night and fired volleys of buckshot into the homes and huts.

Whitecappers Fired Upon Last Night By Negroes.
By Negroes.

Just as The Leader was ready to go to press, a report reached town that Dan Johnson and Link Hudson, two negroes living on the Deloss Peets place in the Red Star neighborhood, had shot into a squad of whitecaps who visited them last night, and it is believed wounded one or more.

Johnson and Hudson were warned before Christmas to leave their houses and a second warning was served a week ago tonight. Instead of leaving after the second warning, the armed themselves with shotguns and waited a return of the whitecaps. Last night, it is said, three of them returned and informed the negroes they had come to make good their threats, when the negroes opened fire at close range and the whitecappers beat a hasty retreat. No further particulars are obtainable.

ARRESTED FOR WHITECAPPING

Ed. Norton and John Falvey, two residents of the Red Star community, were arrested last Saturday on an affidavit sworn out by a negro named Fairman, who lives on the De Loss Peets place, charging them with unlawfully threatening and intimidating himself and other colored people of that community. Norton and Falvey were arrested in Brookhaven where they had been in the habit of coming every few days, and were placed under bonds of $500 each to appear on tomorrow (Thursday) morning for a preliminary hearing before Justice Lanier. Later, Russell Matthews, also charged in the same affidavit with being guilty, was arrested in the country by deputy sheriffs and required to give a similar bond for his appearance tomorrow.

It is understood that at the request of Gov. Longino and the law-abiding citizens of this county, Judge Powell will sit as committing magistrate at this trial and District Attorney Greave, will represent the State. This form of lawlessness is so demors alizing and so destructive of the best interests of the communities where it prevails, and withal so far-reaching in its evil results it is considered that every effort should be made by those in authority and good citizens generally to stamp it out and bring the guilty to justice.

The Leader cannot say in advance of tomorrow's investigation whether the accused are guilty or not, but if they are proven guilty they should be held to the strictest account, and every good citizen of Lincoln county should give his moral and active support, if need be, in seeing that the law is vindicated, not only as regards these men, but all others engaged in carrying on the crimes with which they are charged. There is evidence that, in defiance of the proclamation of the Governor of the State, in defiance of the earnest and solemn protest of the law-abiding citizens of this county, voiced several weeks ago in a mass meeting called for that purpose, the white-cappers have continued to carry on their nefarious and cowardly work in the locality named. It is high time that they were being taught that there is a more potent force in Lincoln county than men who ride around in the dark to frighten harmless negroes, and that that force is the law, represented by the courts, backed up by the moral and patriotic support of every loyal citizen of the county.

Fourteen Whitecaps Indicted and Plead Guilty.
Late this afternoon indictments were returned against 14 members of the whitecap organization. The men charged with this crime, who had previously agreed with the district attorney to plead guilty and throw themselves on the mercy of the court, soon appeared before the bar, were duly arraigned and entered this plea.
In consideration of the fact that, so far as Lincoln county is concerned, the men who joined this organization, did so at a time when there were various sensational rumors started, apparently by labor agents, about "the niggers risin"; that they never actually committed any personal violence; that their lawless acts consisted of a certain form of intimidation, such as riding armed at night, posting up notices and by warning a few negroes regarded as objectionable, to move; that there is no evidence that anything of this kind was done after the Governor issued his proclamation calling upon the members of all such organizations to disband and desist from this lawlessness and the citizens' mass meeting was held in this county denouncing whitecapping; and finally in consideration of the fact that the men indicted had voluntarily surrendered and plead guilty and expressed a willinglenss to respect the law and become good citizens, Judge Powell decided to impose on each one a nominal fine of $5.00 and costs and place them under a bond of $200 each to keep the peace for twelve months.

At the same time the court announced that all members of the organization who would come in and surrender and enter a like plea by tomorrow (Thursday) night, would receive the same lenient treatment; but that all who hung out after that time and had to be hunted up and prosecuted would fare much more severely, a $500 fine and two years in the penitentiary being the extreme limit of the law.

It is believed that what has been done will have the desired effect and assure peace and order in the county, and Judge Powell and District Attorney Greaves are being commended by our best citizens for their action in the premises.

We have on so many occasions been compelled to comment on the failure of authorities in the South to give protection to peaceable negroes against rowdy demonstrations that it is a pleasure to call attention to the prompt and vigorous suppression of Whitecaps in Lincoln County, Miss. Under the Mississippi deed of trust law merchants acquired large tracts of land in that section of the State which were let out to industrious negro farmers. These people excited the jealousy of the "white trash," who consider it a piece of impudence for a negro to be less shiftless than themselves. Last December these tenants received notices from would-be regulators that they would no longer be permitted to cultivate the farms which they had rented. Likewise, many negroes who owned their farms were threatened and calmly told to abandon their homes. This is an old trick, and frequently it is effective. It did not work in this instance, however. What followed is related in a letter to "The Outlook" from a lawyer of Brookhaven, Miss., who is acting for some of the negroes. He writes:

The negroes of Lincoln County complained of this treatment, and the Governor offered a reward for the conviction of persons guilty of giving such notices and making such threats. Affidavits were made against several persons charged with this offence. Afterward they were tried at Brookhaven, the county seat of Lincoln County, by Judge Powell and District Attorney Graves, and they were bound over to await the action of the grand jury. In this trial most of the members of the bar in the county refused to defend the Whitecappers. Upon the meeting of the grand jury the result was that indictments were secured and a conviction followed in each indictment. The judge imposed a fine and put each convicted person under bond to keep the peace. These convictions were secured upon the testimony of two negro men who recognized the Whitecappers upon the night they were warned by said

No demand was made upon the city officers to deliver the negro up to the crowd but the house was guarded on all sides by men who would not allow the negro to be removed from the building. The officers deputized a number of citizens and kept the negro under guard all night.

When the train returned from Columbia with Sheriff Bradford and Prosecuting Attorney Harris, the crowd gathered at the city hall and suddenly the alarm was spread that the negro was gone. The crowd would not believe the statement and at once made a rush into the hall and began a search thru the building. Then a rush was made for the livery stable and mounted men went out in all directions in search of the negro.

W. C. Acuff and Vaughn Hulen went east to Thompson and as they were crossing the track there they met the negro coming in. Mr. Acuff asked him if he would return with them peacably and he said he would. The negro also made the statement that a person came into the room at the city hall where he was confined and told him to make his escape.

CHASE CITY, VA., July 23.—This town was startled this morning by the report of an attempted assault by a negro man on a married lady at her home last night, while her husband was absent at a rehearsal at the town hall.

During the scuffle her screams aroused the children in the house, and their screams, united with hers, attracted attention. Men rushed to her rescue, but the flend escaped in the darkness.

AVERTED

Negroes Suspected of Assault
Taken to Boydton Jail.

ONE MAKES CONFESSION
Citizens of Chase City Met at Dead of Night, but Were Persuaded Not to Act Hastily—Speedy Trial Will Be Had.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

CHASE CITY, VA., July 24.—About 1 o'clock last night many citizens were aroused and informed that one of the prisoners had confessed and a meeting would be held at once near the Banner Warehouse. When I reached the place at 1 o'clock there was a crowd of white men, with arms of different kinds. Some said the law's delay, the possibility of escape and the chances of acquittal on legal technicalities demanded immediate and summary action. But wise counsel prevailed, and a lynching was prevented. Anderson Finch, one of the prisoners, stated that he "went to the house of Mr. C. E. Geoghegon with Dock Bacon, another negro, on the night of the assault; that Bacon went in the porch, while he stood to watch, seized Mrs. Geoghegan, who was sitting there alone, threw meal in her face from a small bag he had with him. A struggle ensued, and during the scuffle with her a child commenced to cry in the house, and fearing from the noise and commotion the neighbors would be aroused, Bacon desisted, and then kicked her, saying: 'Go to your d-d baby! Both then disappeared in the darkness.' This Bacon stoutly denies.

Mrs. Geoghegan remembers the remark made by the negro, but as she was blinded by the meal in her eyes, could not see her asailant. There was a light in the house, which is situated on a public street, with a residence in front and one each to the north and south, not over 100 feet distant. Mrs. Geoghegan was greatly shocked, but not seriously injured.

Finch is a young, black negro, with a bad character and notorious for various offenses.

After a night of excitement a preliminary trial of Finch and Bacon was held early this morning, with the result that both were sent to the county jail, accompanied by a strong guard.

They arrived safely, and the attorney for the Commonwealth promises me that they would be tried by the County Court next Monday or Tuesday.

There is no evidence against Stokes and Dunlop, the other two negroes arrested on suspicion, and they will be released.

UNDER HEAVY GUARD,
Negroes Brought to Boydton by Men Armed With Winchesters.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

BOYDTON, VA., July 24.—The two negro men, Anderson Finch and Dock Bacon, who were arrested yesterday at Chase City, charged with an attempt to criminally assault Mrs. C. E. Geoghegan on Wednesday night, were brought here this morning and lodged in jail. There were twelve men, armed with Winchester rifles, guarding the prisoners.

The guards tell of a very thrilling experience last night, when a lynching party of some seventy-five or a hundred men broke open the Chase City prison and took the men out. The lynching party were, however, persuaded to desist, and they allowed the officers to take charge of their men again. There was intense excitement in town when the prisoners reached here this morning, but no violence was offered, and it is believed that there is no probability of any further trouble, at least, for the present, but all precautions will be taken by the county officials.

Anderson Finch is attempting to fasten the guilt upon Dock Bacon. Since they were brought here this morning Finch told an officer that he was in an adjoining lot to Mr. Geoghegan's, having gone there with Bacon, and that Bacon was the man who went in and made the attack upon the lady; that he had nothing further than that to do with it.

Bacon says that he knows nothing whatever about the matter. It is thought that Finch is trying to clear his skirts.

Commonwealth's Attorney Goode, who has been very active in trying to hunt down the guilty parties, says that a special grand jury will be summoned for to-morrow, and the case will be tried at once if the grand jury brings in a true bill against the prisoners. I was told by one of the guards that there would be other evidence produced at the trial that has not been as yet given to the public, that will tend to fasten the guilt upon the proper man.

There has never been but one lynching in Mecklenburg, and that was of the murderers of the late Dr. Riggins, in the eastern section of the county, some fifteen years ago. The murder was a most brutal affair. There have been six men legally hung in the county since the Civil War.

PETERSBURG, VA., August 3.—The union carpenters and woodworkers employed at the planing mills of Thomas J. Doc Bacon, the Mecklenburg negro, who is now lying in the jail of Mecklenburg county under the shadow of the gallows on which, up to an early hour this morning it was considered inevitable that he was to be hanged to-day, along with another negro, Anderson Finch, convicted of attempted criminal assault, has been granted a few more days of life. DOC BACON
EXECUTED

Protested His Innocence when
on the Scaffold.

NECK BROKEN BY THE FALL
NECK BROKEN BY THE FALL
Large Number of Chase City People Present, and Some of Them Saw the Execution—The Crime for Which He Hung.
BOYDTON, VA., October 3.—Doc. Bacon was hanged here to-day. The trap was sprung at 12:35 P. M. He protested his innocence to the last. When brought upon the scaffold, turning to those in the jail yard, he told them that he knew he was in the face of death, and standing as he was on the death trap, that it was but natural that he should tell the truth. He then most solemnly declared that he was as innocent as it was possible to be.

He said he had no ill will towards the Chase City people, and that he would soon be happy, as he was going home. Some day, he said, the guilty man would be known. Bacon had several colored ministers with him. The body was allowed to hang about twenty-five minutes, when Dr. Hamilton pronounced life extinct.

NECK BROKEN.

The neck was broken by the fall of some six feet, and death was instantaneous, with only one or two convulsive jerks.

Quite a large number of citizens from Chase City were present, some of whom witnessed the execution. The crowd that was here was very orderly, not a single drunken man being seen. Bacon's body was sent on the 3 o'clock train by express to the medical department of the University of Virginia.

This ends one of the most exciting trials and executions ever witnessed in Mecklenburg.

THE CRIME.

The crime for which Doc. Bacon paid the penalty to-day upon the gallows was an attempt to criminally assault Mrs. Charley Geoghegan, at Chase City, some eight or ten weeks ago. The attempt was made about 11 o'clock at night, while her husband was away. The evidence, as given at the trial, was that Bacon, in company with another negro named Anderson Finch, went to Mr. Geoghegan's residence, and while Anderson Finch watched Bacon made the assault, throwing meal into the lady's eyes and seizing her at the same time, and attempted to drag her in a dark part of the porch. The noise aroused her children, and they screamed, frightening the assailant away. Folled in his purpose, he ran off, saying as he left: "Go to your d—n kids!"

THE TRIAL.

Bacon and Finch were tried before the County Court and both found guilty, and Judge Homes sentenced them to be hung on the 2d of September. Finch was hung on that day, but Bacon was respited for two days. At the expiration of the two days, and when all the preparations had been made for the execution, the last religious rites performed, and in fifteen or twenty minutes the death trap would have been sprung, the sheriff received a wire message from the Governor making a second respite, and this time for thirty days. Bacon was sent three times from this place to Petersburg. The hanging to-day was without a hitch.

One man's life paid the penalty and it would appear to the average mind that this would have appeased the appetite of the most blood-thirsty. It is conceded that BACON's conviction was brought about by the testimony of ANDERSON FINCH. His testimony was extorted when the community was in a high state of excitement over the outrage. But when FINCH went to the gallows, he boldly declared that BACON was innocent. ernest-blakeney-lancaster-1903-07-09.A1:
A Negro Enters the Window of A Lady's Room-Cool Heads Prevented Lynching.
Ernest Blakeney, a negro about 19 years of age, was committed to jail here Thursday morning on the charge of entering a dwelling in the night time with the intent to commit an unmentionable crime. About 2 o'clock that morning the negro, who was hired to Mr. J. H. Stewart of O. K., climbed into the bed-room window of Mr. Stewart's daughter by placing two boxes, one on the other, at the outside of the window. As he put one of his feet in to step down to the floor it landed on a trunk which was on rollers and moved making a slight noise awakening the young lady who screamed, causing the negro to jump back to the ground and make a hasty retreat from the premises before her brother, Mr. Rochel Stewart, who was sleeping in an adjoining room and was awakened by her screams, could ascertain from the frightened young lady what the trouble was. The moon was shining bright and the negro was easily recognized by the young lady. Her father and brother failing to overtake him or find him, Mr. Stewart concluded to stand watch at a negro cabin on the plantation where the negro sometimes slept thinking he might endeavor to slip to it before day, while his son went to a neighbors and notified all that he could by phone of the circumstance. By daylight quite a crowd had gathered at Mr. Stewart's to join in the search for the negro when, to their surprise, he came walking up into the yard as though he knew of nothing that had happened. When asked about his conduct he denied any knowledge of the affair but when told he had been recognized by the young lady he confessed everything. When asked his motive he told of his evil purpose in entering the room and it was then for awhile that a lynching seemed imminent. Feeling became intense, not even the people of his own race who were there having any feeling for him, all agreeing that the brute ought to be killed. But, while there were none to pity the miserable wretch there were many men of reason, intelligent, law-abiding men in the crowd, and after a little while they succeeded in prevailing upon the crowd to let the law take its course. The counsels of such men as Abel Funderburk, J. H. Stewart, the father of the young lady, and Rochel Stewart, her brother, a recent honor graduate of North Carolina, and other law-respecting and law-abiding citizens saved that negro's neck, and it isto the everlasting credit of the community that such men are among its citizens. We cannot commend the O. K. people too highly that they have submitted to the majesty of the law when the ends of justice would seemingly have been more speedily met by the rule of the mob. The negro was brought to town and turned over to the sheriff by Rochel Stewart, Abel Funderbunk and B. B. Plyler.

Her father and brother failing to overtake him or find him, Mr. Stewart concluded to stand watch at a negro cabin on the plantation where the negro sometimes slept, thinking he might en deavor to slip to it before day, while his son went to a neighbor's and notified all that he could by phone of the circumstance. By daylight quite a crowd had gathered at Mr. Stewart's to join in the search for the negro when, to their surprise, he came walking up into the yard as though he knew of nothing that had happened. When asked about his conduct he denied any knowledge of the affair but when told he had been recognized by the young lady he confessed everything. When asked his motive he told of his evil purpose in entering the room and it was then for awhile that a lynching seemed imminent. Feeling became intense, not even the people of his own race who were there having any feeling for him, all agreeing that the brute ought to be killed. But, while there were none to pity the miserable wretch there were many men of reason, intelligent law-abiding men in the crowd, and after a little while they succeeded in prevailing upon the crowd to let the law take its course. The counsel of such men as Abel Funderburk, J. H. Stewart, the father of the young lady, and Rochel Stewart, her brother, a recent honor graduate of North Carolina, and other law-respecting and law-abiding citizens saved that negro's neck, and it is to the everlasting credit of the community that such men are among its citizens. We cannot commend the O. K. people too highly that they have submitted to the majesty of the law when the ends of justice would seemingly have been more speedily met by the rule of the mob.

Terrific Explosion.

Frank Roberson Confessed to Burglary and Incendiarism.
A few days since a negro named Frank Roberson was lynched in Arkansas near the Louisiana line. He was an old offender, a bold bad man. The story is soon told. About three years ago a store at Walnut Hill, Ark., was burglarized and fired. Among the contents of the store were two shotguns, one of which was found recently in the possession of a man who on being arrested stated that he had acquired the gun by purchase. With this clue Roberson was apprehended and a rope was placed around his neck. He pleaded for mercy and confessed that he had burglarized and set fire to the store at Walnut Hill. He admitted that he had committed several burglaries and had burned a number of store houses, among which was Belcher's store in Benton, incinerated several years ago. Having admitted his guilt it was decided that he should be lynched, and after a short respite he was jerked to thee limb of a tree, from which the body was found dangling. So has ended the career of a man who for years evaded arrest and had set all law at defiance. He was a menace to any community in which he lived or located temporarily.

Sheriff Garrett Carries Two Unruly Negroes to Jackson to Prevent Mob Violence. Special to the Daily Progress.
Special to the Daily Progress.

Jackson, Sept. 19.—Sheriff Garrett, of Lawrence county, with the assistance of two deputies, has brought to Jackson for safe-keeping two negroes, George and Charlie Pittman. The nergoes were unruly at negro religious services in Lawrence county, and the sheriff was sent for to take them in hand. After his arrival on the scene the negroes turned on the sheriff, and before they could be secured succeeded in wounding him. It seems that the negroes are bad eggs generally, and taking advantage of their latest escapade a lynching party was being formed to pay its respects to them. The sheriff got wind of the matter and hurriedly left the scene with his prisoners for Jackson.

Jonticello Miss Sept 1
Special to Times-Democrat.

Monticello, Miss., Sept. 18.—Charley Pittman and George Pittman, negroes, were hustled out of Monticello last night by officers, who feared their prisoners would be lynched. The two negroes on Sept. 6 resisted arrest and fired on Sheriff Fox and Deputy Garrett. They are alleged to have killed J. L. Nelson near Brookhaven a month ago. Ord Pennington, who was with Nelson at the time he was assassinated came to Monticello Sunday to identify Charles Pittman. He would not say whether the negro was the man or not. That night a mob demanded the jail keys of Sheriff Garrett, who gave it the dodge, after identifying several, and the crowd dispersed. All thought the trouble was over, until it became reported that Mr. Pennington said that Charles Pittman was the negro who murdered Nelson, but that he would not say so to the officers. Last night the attempt at lynching was renewed, but by quick work on the part of the Sheriff and his deputies the negroes' necks were saved.

The store of Mrs. Mary L. Cannon was entered by burglars last night and the safe blown open. The safety vault was not broken into, and very little cash was secured. Hon. G. Wood Magee's horse, bridle and saddle were stolen. The telephone line was cut, and there is no clew as to who did the work.

george-white-wilmington-1903-06-21.A6:
CONFESSED CRIME THURSDAY
White Made Clean Breast to Authorities.
It now transpires that White made a written confession of the crime to the authorities at the workhouse on Thursday, and that the paper is now in the possession of Attorney-General H. H. Ward

This knowledge was withheld from the public for the sole purpose of preventing just what occurred, a lynching. There were rumors to this effect for several days past, but the story, it appears, gained but little headway, and consequently it is safe to say that not 100 men of the great throng who were present at the lynching knew of the confession.

Told Again to Mob.

White told the story of his crime in a corridor on the third floor of the institution where he had been confined. He said in part:

I was sent by Mr. Woodward down to the corn field to thin some corn and I saw Mr. Woodward's daughter and intended to rape her, but a couple of men came along in a wagon and I did not. Then I saw the Bishop girl and I followed her. I seized her and asked if she had any money she would give me to let her go. She gave me half a dollar and two five-cent pieces. Then I seized her and she cried: "Please don't hurt me." I choked her and accomplished my purpose. Then I asked her if she was going to tell on me, and she said she was. Then I gave her a hack in the throat with my knife, and asked her again if she was going to inform on me. She said she was, and then I cut her throat twice again and left her. Then I went back to Mr. Woodward and told him there was no good water to drink down there and he sent me elsewhere. I went back once, but soon left. Then I went back to the house and put on a light hat instead of the cap that I wore. You would not do this if I was a white man and did this. These words corroborate the evidence of Edward Woodward, by whom White was employed, and establishes without doubt the guilt of the unfortunate negro. When the latter was brought downstairs, he remarked: "Now you are all satisfied, deal with me all right." "You will get all that's coming to you." White's only answer was a groan.

White Fought With Desperation.

White fought desperately for his life in the little iron cage cell and knocked down the first man who approached him. The leaders again showed their clear-headedness and one of them, a powerful man, stepped forward before any one could strike the prisoner and threw his arms around the frightened wretch, thus protecting him from violence.

At this time the narrow corridor was so tightly packed by the mob that it was impossible to get the prisoner out. One of the leaders worked his way through the mob to the main corridor and after much difficulty persuaded the crowd to begin the retreat from the building, promising that everybody should get a chance to see the prisoner.

When they did move the crowd cleared the building in a very short time. White, in the custody of two strong men, brought up the rear. The lawn in front of the prison was a sea of faces when viewed from the porch. White's custodians became convinced that unless strategy was used there would be little chance of getting their man to the spot on Price's road where it was planned that the negro should be burned to death.

Lanterns Extinguished.

This danger was overcome by a quiet order to extinguish lanterns or keep them concealed. In the darkness there was a confused rush and after this no one seemed to know where the prisoner was.

On the way White begged to be allowed to say a few words to the crowd before he was killed, and the promise was made to him that he should be allowed to make a statement.

When he found that his case was hopeless the negro confessed to having committed the deed and did not spare himself in telling it. He again confessed as he was standing near a hedge a few feet from where the outrage was committed. He prayed fervently to God to forgive his sins, and seemed anxious to do as much talking as possible in the few minutes he had to live.

Prayed and Confessed.

While White was praying and confessing, and the crowd was struggling to form a circle, three or four stern-faced men began splitting rails with which to burn the wretch. It took so long to get the fuel ready that the crowd impatiently cried to the leaders to proceed with the execution.

The mod numbered from 5,000 to 6,000 persons, who surged back and forth, crowding and pushing, to gain or retain a good position from which to see the burning.

When everything seemed to be about ready a man on a white horse rode into the crowd. It is said his home is in Kentucky. Taking off his broad-brimmed felt hat he bowed to the crowd and said:

"Ladies and gentlemen: Me and this horse are going to get some straw to start this fire."

Torch Applied to Straw.

He rode to a nearby farm house and in a short time reappeared with two stacks of straw. The straw was placed around the stake and White was brought bareheaded into the circle. His nerve seemed to be good and he held his head up while he addressed the crowd.

He made another confession and appealed to God for mercy. A strong rope was then brought and the negro was wrapped in its coils from shoulders to feet. His mouth was working while this was going on and he seemed to be trying to finish his statement. The crowd was in a hurry to get through with its gruesome task and called out for the executioners to hasten. After the rope had been adjusted the negro was fastened to the stake and the torch was applied to the straw.
Rolled in the Flames.

The flames leaped up and licked the man's bare hands. He was held erect by one of the lynchers until his clothing was burning fairly, when he was pushed into the bed of the fire. He rolled about and his contortions were terrible, but he made no sound. Suddenly the ropes on his legs parted and he sprang from the fire and started to run. A man struck him in the head with a piece of fence rail and knocked him down. Willing hands threw him again into the flames. He rolled out several times, but was promptly returned. While this was going on shouts, cheers and jibes went up from the crowd.

When the negro had ceased to show sign of life the body was placed on its back and fuel was piled upon it until a roaring fire was soon consuming it. It was about 2 o'clock when the crowd began to disperse.

Greusome Relics Taken.

At noon today Deputy Coroner Killmer went to the scene of the lynching for the purpose of securing some of the remains of the negro, so as to go through the legal form of holding an inquest. But according to the story of those who had left the place an hour previous there was little probability of his finding anything substantial, as the relic-hunters had made off with the pieces of bones that were left.

Preacher Makes Statement.

The Rev. Mr. Ellwood of the Presbyterian church, who last Sunday forcefully expressed himself in a sermon appealing to the justices of the Supreme court for an immediate trial of White, dictated the following statement:

"I am very sorry this happened as it did. I believe the man should have had a legal trial, but I also believe he should have had a speedy trial. QUIET IN DELAWARE
RELEASE OF CORWELL CALMS ANGRY AND DESPERATE MOB.
No Punishment Likely for Men Who Burned the Negro White at Stake.
WILMINGTON, Del., June 25.—The verdict of the coroner's jury in the case of George White, the negro who was burned at the stake, and the release of Arthur Corwell on bail seem to have appeased the unruly element here. For a time last night there appeared to be danger of race riots, but when it became generally known that Corwell had been discharged from custody all disturbances ceased and everything is quiet today.

Corwell protests that he was not present at the lynching. No other arrests have been made.

Corwell claims to live in Hartford city, Ind.

Coroner McCormick held two sessions in the inquest on the remains of White yesterday, the first bringing to light a difference of opinion between the coroner and his deputy, John R. Kilmer, which resulted in an open clash. Kilmer thought that Attorney General H. Hif Ward should have selected the jury, while the coroner maintained that the attorney general had no authority in the matter. The coroner carried out his plan and impaneled a jury.

Five Pounds of Flesh.

When the inquest began the remains of White could not be found, and after a long search they were found wrapped in paper on an ice chest. White weighed about 200 pounds, but only five pounds of flesh and bone were left of him after the lynchers had concluded their work.

With the finding of the remains, the coroner discovered that no witnesses were present. He consulted with his deputy, who told him he did not approve of the haste and of the manner in selecting the jury, and, therefore, could give him no assistance.

"Where can I get witnesses?" asked the coroner.

"Hunt around," was his deputy's reply. The coroner replied that he was not going to let the attorney general run his business, and Kilmer retorted that the attorney general was not trying to run the inquest. At this juncture the inquest was adjourned, to convene at the call of the coroner.

Inquest on Bones.

Later on the coroner again summoned the jury and the inquest was held last night. Thomas Leach, a farmer, and William Carter, a newspaper reporter, were the witnesses, and both testified to the finding of the small portion of the remains of the victim of the mob. Some further testimony was offered, after which the jury brought in the following verdict:

"Resolved, That George White came to his death between the hours of 10 p.m. of June 22, 1903, and 4 a.m. of June 23, 1903, by being burned in a field adjoining the road leading from Price's Corner to the Ferris Industrial School, by a party or parties unknown to this jury."

The belief is growing here that no one will ever be punished for the work of the mob. Certain prominent citizens, although they deplore the occurrence, stand ready to raise a fund for the defense of any one who should be prosecuted for the offense.

ARREST LYNCHERS.
Delaware Authorities Decide That They Will Prosecute Slayers of George White.

Wilmington, Del., June 24.—The arrest of Arthur Corwell, who was taken into custody last night on suspicion of being implicated in the lynching of George White, the Negro murderer of Miss Bishop, is the only one made thus far. The arrest was made at the instance of Attorney General Ward. Corwell will be arraigned for a preliminary hearing on a charge of murder as soon as the state authorities can make the necessary arrangements.

It is expected that other arrests will follow, but the attorney general said today that no additional warrants had been issued and he did not know whether any more would be sworn out.

Peter Smith, the boy who was shot during the mob's attack on the workhouse Monday night, died at the hospital at 2 o'clock this afternoon.

A Mighty Delaware Mob Storms the Workhouse.
WENT THROUGH A HAIL OF BULLETS. Four Thousand Desperate Men Led by a Virginian Avenge the Murder of Miss Bishop—At I o'Clock in the Morning They Take the Negro From the Workhouse, and After He Confesses Burn Him. Wilmington, Del. (Special).—A Delaware mob, led by a Virginian, burned a negro at the stake within a few miles of Mason and Dixon's line. The victim was George White, a negro, who feloniously assaulted and then stabbed to death Miss Helen S. Bishop, the 17-year-old daughter of Rev. Dr. E. A. Bishop. The crime was committed Monday afternoon, June 15, and ever since that time there had been threats of synching. An effort was made to take White from the New Castle county work-house, where he was held a prisoner, but it failed. Monday night, as a result of the law's slowness and of agitation on the part of those who cried for vengeance, a mob that was estimated at 4,000 men and boys gathered in the neighborhood of Price's Corner, four miles from Wilmington. They came from everywhere, including Wilmington and the small towns south of Price's Corner. The previous lack of a leader was supplied by a Virginian, whose identity in the confusion and excitement could not be learned. The police of Wilmington and the county constables tried to disperse the growing mob, but without avail. It was evident that hundreds came from mere curiosity, but once in the mob they became inflamed with the spirit pervading the throng and then actively joined it. The active spirits were few in number, but they did their work well. It was after 10 o'clock when the march to the workhouse, a mile away, was taken up. The chief warden of the workhouse and his guards, who had been on almost constant duty since the negro was landed in the prison, had been warned of the coming of the mob and prepared to defend White at all costs. REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

Armstrong, Mo., June 14.—Henry Meredith, a negro boy, who was arrested Saturday by Constable Morehead charged with cutting Will Boggs, another negro, was taken from the city jail Saturday by a posse of citizens and severely whipped with harness tugs.

The jail door was broken open and the negro was taken about one-half mile from town, tled to a telegraph pole and given 150 lashes with a harness tug, his outer garments having been stripped from his body.

He had just served a term in the State Reform School at Boonville for attempting to wreck an Alton passenger train by piling railroad ties on the track.

WERE AFTER THE "BUNGALOOS."
100 Special Policemen Sworn In to Guard Indianapolis Negroes.
INDIANAPOLIS, June 14.—One hundred special policemen were appointed to-day to guard the several parks of the city in anticipation of a clash between whites and negroes and, in charge of experienced officers, were on duty at Riverside, Fairview, Garfield and Military parks.

Two years ago a "Bungaloo" gang was organized among white toughs, and last season they gave the police a great deal of trouble by their attacks upon negroes who frequented the parks. The negroes had given no cause of offence, but many of them armed themselves and determined not to be driven out of the parks. Clashes followed and the "Bungaloo" and negroes began to increase until a race war seemed inevitable.

Appeals were made to the police by older and more conservative colored men, and the Mayor at last ordered the police superintendent to protect the colored youths at all hazards.

Yesterday the police were told of a plot on the part of the "Bungaloo" to make trouble to-night, and the special officers were sworn in so as to have a force on hand that would be able to cope with the situation. Many of the negroes went to the parks this evening determined to defend themselves against attack, but the hoodlum element refrained from violence.

"BUNGALOOISM."
Students of sociology have noted that large cities are subject to various "waves" of crime, general outbreaks that sometimes have a logical cause in reigning conditions, but more frequently have no other cause than the power of example. Thus there will be a series of murders committed by different people, a general prevalence of petty thieving or an outbreak of rowdyism, such as the celebrated wave of "Hooliganism" which bade fair to swamp the London constabulary in 1900.

To combat some such wave the Indianapolis police authorities have found it necessary to adopt stern repressive measures against what is locally known as "bungalooism." Additional sergeants have been appointed and orders issued to officers and patrolmen to act promptly and strenuously at the first approach toward hoodlum tactics in any quarter. Some years ago there were a couple of small gangs of hoodlums in Indianapolis known as "the Boo Gang," with its center of activity in the southeastern part of the city and its activities largely devoted to beer-drinking in the railroad yards, and "the Bungaloo Gang," which operated in the northwestern part of town and came into occasional clash with negroes on Indiana avenue.

Both of these gangs have long since dispersed, but the word "Bungaloo" has survived as a rallying cry for any crowd of rowdies that may collect in any part of the city. Race prejudice bobs up frequently and there are frequent attacks on negroes to record; especially in the northwestern part of the city, but "Bungalooism" is not practiced on negroes alone, as a good many broken heads of white men will testify. Almost invariably the participants in these little riots are irresponsible boys in their later 'teens, and, while the damage has never, as yet, been very great, the outbreaks have occasionally looked very serious. The spirit of riot and mob violence grows, of course, with great rapidity, and the police are moving none too soon in their special effort to repress it. A few penitentiary sentences for assault with intent to kill will have a very salutary effect in making these lads stop to think before rushing pell-mell into the first trouble that presents itself.

Austin, Tex., Oct. 14.—General Webster Flanagan, United States collector of internal revenue for this district, to-day appealed to Governor Lanham that the State give protection to the negroes of Rusk County and aid in bringing to justice white men guilty of torturing to death an inoffensive negro.

TORTURE OF NEGROES.
Collector Flanagan Reports Terrible Crueltles Perpetrated in Rusk County. Tex.
AUSTIN, Tex., Oct. 14.—Webster Fianagan, United States Collector of Internal Revenue for this district, returned to-day from Rusk county, in this State, where he went several days ago to investigate the murders and cruelties that are being perpetrated upon the negroes of that county by bands of white men.

"No one can portray the cruelties to which the negroes of Rusk county have been subjected during the past several weeks," Mr. Flanagan said to-day. "I have laid the matter before Gov. Lanham, with a view of bringing about the punishment of those who are guilty. If necessary, an appeal will be made to the Federal authorities.

"A few nights before my visit to the county two of the most peaceable and inoffensive negroes were taken from their homes by a band of white men. They were stripped and tied to trees and then whipped with the most terrible instrument of torture ever devised by savage man. This instrument was a broad strip of rawhide fastened on to an oak handle. Nails were driven through the rawhide, protruding nearly a half inch. The negroes were whipped into insensibility with these lashes, each stroke driving the nails into the cringing body. One of these negroes died last Saturday night from his injuries and the other one is in a critical condition. The men who committed this crime are well known. Four of them have been arrested.

"The order has gone forth that all negroes must leave the county. The only excuse given for the murder and outrages that have been committed is that it is a white man's county. Many negroes have obeyed the warning and moved away."

john-revel-new-york-1903-12-12.A1:
ATTEMPT TO LYNCH
NEGRO IN NEW YORK
New York, December 14.—An angry crowd tried to take John Revel, a young negro, from the police early Saturday, at the corner of Twenty-eighth street and Eighth avenue, and hang him to a lamp-post. He had shot Katherine Miller, an old woman of his race, probably fatally, and Agnes Brennan, who had been an innocent spectator of his attempt.

"Lynch him! Lynch him!" the crowd cried. 'Hang him to a lamp-post!" and they closed in on the would-be murderer.

"Hang him! hang him up to the lamp-post!" shouted a wildeyed fellow, who had all the elements of a riotmaker in him, and the cry was taken up again. It was time to call a halt, and the police drew their pistols and leveled them at the leaders of the crowd, who were pressing in on them. The sight of the revolvers had their effect on the majority of those who were yelling for a lynching, and the fell back, but half a dozen bolder spirits were not easily awed and they did not break ground until they were told they would be shot if they did not open a way for Revel and his captors.

MOB HANGS FOR KILLING Negro Seizes the Jailor Intending to Escape. TWO WHITE YOUTHS AID Sheriff Is Made Prisoner and His Hands Tied. CROWD DECIDES TO LYNCH Fire Company Refuses to Help Disperse the Mob.
Hattiesburg, Miss., Aug. —A negro, Amos Jones, was hanged by a mob here tonight for shooting and mortally wounding Jailer M. M. Sexton. Jones and another negro, named McElroy, who were prisoners, seized Sexton, intending to break from the jail. McElroy threw Sexton down, and two white youths, also prisoners, held him. The negroes disarmed Sexton and Jones shot him, inflicting three wounds that are said to be fatal. A crowd gathered outside the jail, while a deputy and several others entered and overpowered three of the prisoners. In the confusion McElroy escaped from the jail. The crowd outside decided to lynch Jones. Prominent men urged them to desist and the wounded jailer sent word to leave the man unharmed. The mob later seized Sheriff Batson and tied him. The fire brigade was requested to trun out and help disperse the mob, but refused. The mob then broke into a window of the jail and cut the negro out of his cell with chisels. He was brought out to the crowd of about 500 men and boys, a rope was tied around his neck and he was dragged through the town to Gordon creek bridge, where he was hanged to a telegraph pole and bullets were fired into his body. It is thought he was dead before he was hanged. The sheriff had telegraphed to the governor when the mob first assembled and an order came to the local militia to turn out, but it was too late. While the mob was forming and threatening to lynch the white prisoners also, the sheriff spirited them out of town.

THEY UTTER THREATS.

Valparaiso, Ind., Aug. 8. —John Wilson, a powerful negro, this afternoon attempted to assault Mrs. Hugh F. Bitt, at her home, four miles in the country. She was in the house with her two little children when the negro appeared at the door and asked for matches. When he attacked her the children screamed and the negro ran. Over a hundred neighboring farmers and farmers' hands started in pursuit. The negro jumped a passing freight train and escaped to Warsaw. The telephone had been used and Deputy Sheriff Matthews and William Wilson, a school teacher, were at the depot. The negro drew a knife and attacked Matthews, but was knocked unconscious by a stone thrown by Wilson. He confessed.

Tonight the streets of the town have been filled with angry farmers of Washington township, muttering threats of vengeance, but no attack on the jail is feared.
