Captured After a Chase, and Taken to the Seat of Porter County, Where He Is Now Held.
LYNCHING IN MISSISSIPPI
COLD CHISELS USED BY A MOB TO ENTER A NEGRO'S CELL.
Victim Dragged Through a Town, Hanged to a Telegraph Pole and His Body "Riddled."
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

VALPARAISO, Ind., Aug. 8.—For a time to-night it was feared an attempt would be made to lynch a negro who is in jail here under guard. The determined stand taken by the sheriff, however, cooled the ardor of the would-be lynchers, and at midnight all was quiet on the streets.

About 4 o'clock this afternoon, while Mrs. U. S. Biggs, a young woman thirty years of age, who is the wife of a Washington township, Porter county, farmer, was alone at her home with two small children, a negro, who afterwards gave his name to the authorities as John Wilson, and a stranger, came to the door and asked for matches to go to a field to roast some corn. He later returned and asked for salt and pepper. While on this trip Wilson caught Mrs. Biggs by the throat and choked and kicked her while attempting to criminally assault her. Mrs. Biggs is now in a very critical condition.

When the crime became known relatives and farmers in the vicinity, armed with shotguns, formed a posse of nearly 100, which started in pursuit of the negro.

At Winslow Station, the nearest village, the telephone was used to notify officers in surrounding towns of the crime. The negro escaped the posse, jumped on a freight train and went to Wanatah, ten miles west of Valparaiso. Here Deputy Sheriffs Matthews and Billy Wilson, the latter a school teacherj and pugilist, saw the negro and ordered him to stop. The negro drew a long knife and threatened to kill them. Wilson picked up a stone, struck the negro and felled him to the ground.

Matthews and Wilson brought the negro to the county jail here while Sheriff Lacount and a score of deputies were searching the roads. The prisoner arrived at the jail here at 8:30 to-night and gave his name as John Wilson, saying he was from Pittsburg, Pa., and that he had been working on the railroad. At the jail Wilson was surly and declined to talk of the affair, although asking queer questions. The officers believe he is feigning insanity. Farmers living in the vicinity of the Biggs home and people here are greatly incensed and neighbors and Biggs's friends threaten violence.

Sheriff Lacount said to-night: "I do not fear an outbreak of a mob, but if there is I have a dozen armed men here in case of mob violence."

At 9 o'clock the negro confessed to Sheriff Lacount that he committed assault and battery, but denied having ravished the woman.

At 11 o'clock there was still some talk of lynching the negro, but at midnight there were few pqpeople on the streets. The jail force was doubled. Lack of a leader undoubtedly prevented an attempt to take the negro by force. A number of farmers bought cartrides at the stores to-night and a business man offered to furnish rope, but the crowd lacked a leader.
john-wilson-valparaiso-1903-08-08.A8:
NEGRO WILSON IS SAFE
NO FURTHER ATTEMPT TO FORM A MOB AT VALPARAISO.
Sheriff La Count Prepared to Hurry Mrs. Biggs's Assailant Out of the City if Necessary.
VALPARAISO, Ind., Aug. 9.—While there is no apparent sign of a further attempt to wreak mob violence on the negro John Wilson, who assaulted Mrs. U. S. Biggs, white, the wife of a young farmer five miles southeast of here Saturday afternoon, the people of this city and the vicinity where the affair occurred are much wrought up. Sheriff La Count, however, is confident there will be no trouble and to make sure he scoured the country surrounding the city this evening to see if any plans were being made to lynch the negro. Matters were quiet during the day, but if signs of trouble should develop the prisoner will be taken to either Michigan City or Laporte.

The condition of Mrs. Biggs to-day was critical and her recovery is doubtful. People living near the Biggs home stated today that if the farmers' posse had got hold of the negro before the authorities they would have made quick work of him. Mrs. Biggs's throat bears marks where the negro fastened his fingers and her limbs are lacerated.

While prominent citizens regret the outrage they are expressing gratitude that no mob violence occurred. They have been urging the people to let the law take its course, but are hoping for speedy action and the full limit of punishment for the crime. Pastors of the local churches in their comments to-day uttered the same sentiments.
john-wilson-valparaiso-1903-08-08.A9:
SHERIFF NOT ALARMED
VALPARAISO OFFICER DOES NOT ANTICIPATE TROUBLE.
The Negro Wilson Laughed in Telling of Escape from Posse of Farmers.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

VALPARAISO, Ind., Aug. 10.—John Wilson, the negro who assaulted and nearly killed Mrs. Biggs last Saturday afternoon while she was alone at her country home, five miles east of here, remains in jail. Sheriff Lacount anticipates no trouble, and does not see anything to warrant the removal of the prisoner. He stated to-night, however, that he would keep the armed guards at the jail to-night in the event trouble should arise. Prosecutor Mitchell to-day investigated the case, and found the woman in a worse condition than the public was allowed to know of, it being publicly announced by the authorities that she would recover, so that the enraged neighbors would allow their high feeling to subside. In fact, the woman is in a precarious condition. The negro was to have been given a preliminary hearing to-day, but Mrs. Biggs was in no condition to leave her bed to appear against him. When Wilson was interview to-day he told of his escape from the posse of enraged farmers who sought his life, and, being safe in jail, he laughed. He talks but little and is of a surly disposition. He is about six feet tall and weighs 190 pounds. Sheriff Lacount this evening received a telegram from Pittsburg, Pa., that a negro answering Wilson's description is wanted in Allegheny county for an offense committed there over a year ago.
john-wilson-valparaiso-1903-08-08.A10:
RUMOR THAT NEGRO WAS TO BE MOVED FROM VALPARAISO JAIL. Condition of Mrs. U. S. Biggs, Wilson's Victim, Is Serious-Attempt to Wreck Traction Car.
VALPARAISO, Ind., Aug. 11.—The condition of Mrs. U. S. Biggs was reported as serious to-day, as she is suffering much from her wounds. The attending physicians say that she may never be able to appear against her assailant in court, in which case speedy justice will be materially delayed. William Meadow, of Michigan City, father of Mrs. Biggs, was called to-day to his daughter's bedside.

Feeling against John Wilson, the negro now in custody for his attempted assault on Mrs. Biggs, has not calmed down as yet, as was demonstrated late last night, when a rumor that Wilson was to be removed to the State prison at Michigan City reached the Biggs neighborhood, where the assault occurred. The news was spread and a crowd of armed farmers, friends of Biggs, waited along the roadside hoping for this chance to get the prisoner while out of jail. The incensed feeling has caused a number of negroes to leave the city for Chicago and two negroes in business were practically forced to suspend.

The bitter feeling in the case is made all the more stronger because of a brutal attempt at rape here several months ago, when Charles Lybarges, alias Burch, a local character, assaulted Miss Bertha Harrold, of this city, while she was in the act of planting flowers on the graves of her dead father and mother at a cemetery on the edge of town. Lybarges escaped only by fleeing into Michigan, where he was afterward caught and sentenced to prison. Miss Harrold has been in a hospital since that time.
john-wilson-valparaiso-1903-08-08.A12:
Threatened Lynching at Valparaiso.
The streets of Valparaiso were crowded Saturday night with angry farmers of Washington township, who threatened to lynch John Wilson colored, who attempted to assault Mrs. Hugh F. Bitts.

The crime occurred about 4 o'clock on the Bitts farm, in Washington township, Porter county, five miles west of Valparaiso. Mrs. Bitts, with her two little children, was in the house at work, when the negro, a powerfully built man, appeared in the door and asked for matches. He said he wished to roast some corn in a field nearby.

After a few minutes he appeared in the door again and, when Mrs. Bitts opened it, asked for some salt and pepper. The woman went to get them, and the negro grasped her by the throat and attempted to choke her. The woman's struggles to be free were fruitless against the powerful strength of the colored man. The little children, who were in the house, cried out in fear and frightened the negro away.

The latter was being hotly pursued when he caught the Pennsylvania freight train, half a mile south of the Bitts homestead, and went to Warsaw. The officials there had been warned, and Deputy Sheriff Mathews and "Bill" Wilson, a well-known athlete, met the negro at the train at 7 o'clock.

The colored man drew a knife and rushed upon Mathews, when Wilson felled him with a heavy stone. He was immediately bound and gagged taken to Valparaiso and lodged in jail at 7:30 Saturday evening.

Inside of an hour the streets were crowded with the angry farmers of Washington township bent upon dealing summary punishment to the colored men but better counsel prevailed and the law will be allowed to take its course.
john-wilson-valparaiso-1903-08-08.A17:
WANTS NO MORE NEGROES.
An Indiana Republican Opposes Bringing Any More to His State.
LAPORTE, Ind., Aug. 16.—Arthur J. Bowser, editor of the Chesterton Tribune, clerk in the State Legislature and a well-known Republican in Porter county, has taken the initiative in organizing opposition to the settlement of negroes in this county and in northwestern Indiana. Last Saturday a negro tramp assaulted a farmer's wife near Valparaiso and seriously injured her. All day Sunday the streets were filled with angry farmers and college students, threatening to break the jail and lynch the negro, who admitted the crime. That crime brought out Bowser's proposition.

Bowser admits that he has always entertained a deep-rooted antipathy toward the negro race and declares that it is now time for communities having few colored citizens to protect themselves against any further increase from Southern States. He says:

"The settlement of negroes from the South in this county means that fear would enter the home of every farmer in the county and our wives, daughters and sweethearts would be exposed to a fate more horrible than death in any form, property values would go down and lynchings would follow."
john-wilson-valparaiso-1903-08-08.A18:
BOLD EDITOR'S VIEWS. Discourges the Settlement of Negroes in Porter County.
VALPARAISO, Ind., Aug. 17.—Editor A. J. Bowser, of the Chesterton Tribune, this county, has taken the initiative in an organized opposition to the settlement of negroes in Porter county, where a colored man, John Wilson, last week narrowly escaped lynching for assaulting Mrs. U. S. Biggs, the wife of a farmer. He says editorially: "The settlement of negroes from the South in this county means that fear would enter the home of every farmer in the county, and our wives, daughters and sweethearts would be exposed to a fate more horrible than death in any form, property values would go down and lynchings would follow." The proposition is to discourage in effective ways all negroes from locating within the county.

An Unidentified Demented Man.

LEBANON, Ind., Aug. 17.—A strange insane man is in the Boone County Infirmary awaiting the efforts of the authorities to identify him. When arrested he claimed he was a lecturer and had lived in the world a million years and in the flesh seventy-three years. He said his name was William Henderson, and then declared there was nothing in a name. He wears good clothes, and has a grip containing a Prince Albert suit. He is about fifty years of age. His collars are marked "William B. O'Conner," but he says this is not his name. Among his possessions are a Bible and a picture of William McKinley.

Wayne County Rural Carriers.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

RICHMOND, Ind., Aug. 17.—The rural mail carriers of Wayne county met in this city and completed an organization to be known as a branch of the Indiana Rural Carriers' Association. The only work done at the first meeting was to complete the organization. Harry Fisher, Richmond, was chosen president; Oscar Werking, Hagerstown, vice president; A. C. Walker, Hagerstown, secretary; Richard L. Walker, Cambridge City, treasurer; John L. Du Granrut, Milton, corresponding secretary; Harry Fisher, Richmond, delegate to state convention.

Indiana Weddings.

HARRIS—BINKLEY.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

TIPTON, Ind., Aug. 17.—Miss Clara Binkley, daughter of Mr. and Mrs., Henry Binkley, and Fremont Harris, of Indianapolis, were married at the home of the bride's parents, on South East street, yesterday. Only the immediate relatives of the bride were present, and the marriage was a surprise to the friends of the bride in this city. The Rev. U. S. A. Bridge, pastor of the Main-street Methodist Church, performed the ceremony. They will live in Indianapolis.

Relatives Unable to Agree.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

LAPORTE, Ind., Aug. 17.—Balsar Crane and Oscar McCormick have begun proceedings in Laporte Circuit Court to have Henry P. Crane, a respected and wealthy Laporte county farmer, adjudged of unsound mind and a receiver appointed for his estate on the ground that he is incapable of managing the same. Other relatives will contest the appointment of a receiver, so that a lively legal battle is anticipated. Crane is well advanced in years and has been in feeble health for some time.

Big Mortgage Lifted.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

MUNCIE, Ind., Aug. 17.—The Union Trust Company of Indianapolis filed notice to-day of the release of a $60,000 mortgage held on the property of the Heat, Light and Power Company of this city. The amount has been paid in full.
john-wilson-valparaiso-1903-08-08.A19:
WILSON QUIETLY ARRAIGNED.
Assailant of Porter County Woman Bound Over.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

VALPARAISO, Ind., Aug. 22.—John Wilson, the negro who assaulted Mrs. U. S. Biggs, of this county, was taken out of jail quietly this evening without the public knowing of the fact and given a preliminary hearing. He pleaded not guilty, and was bound over to the next term of court under $5,000 bond. GIVEN THE LIMIT.
Valparaiso Negro Sentenced to Prison for Assaulting Mrs. Biggs.
for Assaulting Mrs. Biggs.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

VALPARAISO, Ind., Oct. 6.—John Wilson, the burly negro who viciously assaulted Mrs. U. S. Biggs on Aug. 7 was given the full extent of the law in the Porter Superior Court this morning by Judge Tuthill. After hearing the evidence of a dozen witnesses Judge Tuthill did not care to hear argument and pronounced sentence. Wilson gets the limit, two to fourteen years in the State prison at Michigan City, also a fine of $10 and costs. Wilson gave his age as twenty-four, but Judge Tuthill placed it at 30, so the prisoner goes to the Prison North instead of the Reformatory at Jeffersonville. Wilson, who entered a plea of not guilty, fought the case on the ground that another negro committed the act.

Gould Run Down Stray Horse with Their Machine in the Dark and Are Found Unconscious.
There is a slight improvement to-day in the condition of Mr. and Mrs. Charles A. Gould, who were thrown out when their big gasoline automobile ran into a horse near their Bayside, L. I., home. Dr. Charles Story told an Evening World reporter to-day that he now hoped for their recovery and that their injuries were not quite so serious as he at first thought.

Two other physicians were called to assist Dr. Story. They worked over the injured man and woman almost all night, and it was almost daylight before they were restored to consciousness. They are still at "The Willows," the summer home of John W. Harway, where they were carried after the accident.

The Goulds occupy a handsome home just outside of Bayside, on the Bell road. Mrs. Gould is the daughter of Richard M. Bell, an old and wealthy resident of the town.

They started out alone last night in their big gasoline touring car. Mr. Gould running the machine. They covered many miles along the moonlit roads and started to return home shortly before midnight.

They were descending a long hill, which terminates in a turn in front of their home. The road seemed clear and Gould was giving the machine full speed in a delightful whirl down the decline.

Just as they got to the curve, which is but slight, a horse that had apparently escaped from a near-by pasture jumped out into the road directly in front of the speeding car. There was no chance of escape. The big machine hit the horse, killing it instantly.

The auto jumped over the horse's body, and the collision pitched Mr. Gould and his wife out headlong on the road. They fell with great force and lay unconscious.

Mr. Gould, in the second he saw the danger, had shut off the power, but the automobile was carried half way up an opposite hill by the momentum before it came to a stop.

A hundred feet away from the point of the accident is the home of John W. Harway, the Willows. The Harway family heard the screams of Mrs. Gould, followed by the crash, and ran out. They carried the unconscious forms of the man and wife into the house.

RACE RIOT FEARED IN OHIO.
Mob Wanted to Lynch Negro Accused of Assaulting White Girl.

maynard-hudson-hillsboro-1903-08-08.A20:
OHIO MOB CAME ARMED.
Negro Had Been Taken Away, But the Men Went Through the Jail.
Hillsboro, O., Aug. 13.—At an early hour this morning a mob of about 200 masked men attacked the county jail to lynch Maynard Hudson, the negro who is charged with attempting to assault a white girl named Hindman. Sheriff Elton had received an intimation that the mob would likely come and took the negro out of jail quietly and went across country with him to Leesburg, where he now is.

The white men were badly battered up and one of them, Charles Kiernan, of No. 420 West Forty-seventh street, was arrested on complaint of Mingo Hamilton, a negro, who lives at No. 512 West Fifty-fifth street.

There are four houses in the block occupied exclusively by negroes. The advent of negroes into the neighborhood aroused the resentment of the whites. Who have been living around there for years, and fights have been frequent. Lately they have become bitter contests in which knives were used.

Last Saturday night Mingo Hamilton was sitting on his front stoop, blissfully contemplating a can of beer at his side, when along came a crowd of young white men. The cry acted as an alarm. A-black cloud poured out of the tenements. In less than a minute Kiernan and his companions were fighting for their lives. The negro women ran out of the house with knives and clubs for the men and the shouts of the rioters could be heard at Ninth avenue.

A neighbor telephoned to Police Headquarters and the reserves were hustled from the West Forty-seventh street station to the scene. By this time Kiernan was about tuckered out. Negro Employed by Coast Line Quit Because One of Them Was Mobbed.

Because a negro cursed one of the workmen in the Atlantic Coast Line shops at Wilmington, N. C., Thursday, over two hundred fellow workmen almost mobbed him at the noon hour when all the men knocked off for dinner. The negro, whose name is Sanders, was badly beaten, but no very serious injury resulted.

Sanders, with 500 other negroes, is employed about the shops to do heavy work. As a result of the trouble the entire force of negroes walked out and refused to work the remainder of the day. Just what the outcome will be is not known, but the Coast Line management started an investigation at once and will probe the matter to the bottom. It is rumored that trouble between the two races has been brewing for some time.

SEVEN NEGROES SHANGHAIED.
Put Aboard a Russian Bark at Savannah and Landed in Bristol, England.
Put Aboard a Russian Bark at Savannah and Landed in Bristol, England.

SAVANNAH, Ga., Sept. 26.—Harry Olsen, already under bond for having shanghaied two youths in Savannah and shipping them to the unhealthy port of Santos, Brazil, was taken in the toils again to-day by a Deputy United States Marshal. With him in his latest trouble is Jack Johnson, a negro.

The men were charged with luring aboard the Russian bark Alice seven able-bodied men who knew nothing of ships or life at sea and shipping them without their consent on the bark for the long voyage to Bristol, England.

The men are all from Savannah and are now in Bristol, where they are dependent on charity. Their case was investigated by United States Consul Lathrop at Bristol, and upon his report the Government determined to proceed against Olsen and Johnson.

The shanghaied men charge in an affidavit, now in Savannah, that on July 9 last they were asked by Johnson to go down the river on a tug to do some work. They were not sailors and had no idea that they were to be shipped aboard a vessel.

On the way to Tybee Road they were made drunk and when the Alice was reached they had the alternative of sailing on her or being put off into the water. They were asked to sign articles but declined, and the bark sailed with them protesting.

At sea, they say, they were treated cruelly, and when Bristol was reached, instead of being paid, they were told that they owed the ship's master $5 each, as they had not earned as much as had been paid to the sailor runner in Savannah for them. The men appealed for aid in Bristol and were referred to the United States Consul, who investigated their case and had the officers at Washington take action.

There has been filed here a copy of a receipt given by the master of the Alice to Olsen for $200 for the seven men. The men are all negroes.

This method of obtaining labor on the coast is worse than peonage in the interior of the State.

The case against Olsen will be tried before Judge Emory Speer of the United States Court after an investigation by a United States Commissioner. Judge Speer has shown by heavy fines in the recent peonage cases how he feels toward men who deprive others of their liberty and independence.
savannah-savannah-1903-09.A4:
HE'S NO SHANGHAIER
SAYS OLSEN, BUT HE GAVE $1,600 BOND.
TO ANSWER FOR KIDNAPPING
EIGHT SAVANNAH NEGROES WHOM HE SOLD INTO SERVITUDE.
Harry Olsen and Jack Johnson Arrested by U. S. Authorities—Negroes Sold to Austrian Bark Alice and Taken to Bristol—Olsen Received $200—Says It Was Expense Money—Shanghai Negroes Atrociously Treated and Discharged at Bristol Without a Cent—Taken in Charge by American Consul.

Harry Olsen, who was arrested yesterday under eight warrants, sworn out by United States Assistant District Attorney Alexander Akerman, under direction of the Attorney General, was released from jail under a $1,600 bond last night.

Olsen, together with a negro named Jack Johnson, who was arrested at the same time, is charged with kidnapping eight Savannah negroes and selling them to the officers of the Russian bark Alice, on which they were transported to Bristol, England, and discharged without a cent. The negroes claim that they were forced aboard the Russian bark, and were made to perform the most menial labor at the point of a pistol.

The account of their sale into servitude and the atrocities practiced upon them are contained in affidavits made before United States Consul Lathrop at Bristol, which were forwarded to the State Department, and by the officials sent to Mr. Akerman. The names of the eight negroes are John Porter, Joe Easterlin, Jesse Hall, William Jones, James Gillard, Ben Mani-gault, Moses Smallwood and Benty Washington. Nearly all of them are young boys.

The Negroes' Story.

The negroes, according to their stories, were approached by Johnson, a runner of Olsen's, and offered jobs of loading lumber at Sapelo. Anxious to make a little money they went with Johnson down the river. The trip was made on a tug, on which Olsen was in charge. When Sapelo was reached they were ordered to board the Alice, and on refusing were told that they would have to swim ashore if they didn't.

Capt. Granit of the Alice gave Olsen $200 for the men, for which Olsen gave a receipt, which is now in the hands of the district attorney. Olsen acknowledges the receipt of the money, but says that it was spent, in great part, in buying clothes for the men and in paying the expenses of the tug down the river. The negroes, when arrested in Bristol, were ragged and dirty and there was not a soul in the crowd.

They tell of the most awful atrocities. They say that they were beaten with heavy irons and kicked until they feared they would die. In this sort of treatment the officers delighted. When Bristol was reached they asked for their wages, when Capt. Granit told them that far from being in their debt, they owed him $5 each.

Under Protection of Consul.

The double quartette of ebony-hued Americans were taken under the protection of the American consulate. They will be transported back to Savannah as soon as may be. The State Department referred the matter to the Department of Justice and the Attorney General, in turn, referred it to Mr. Akerman.

Olsen and Johnson were arrested by Deputy Marshals Wilson and Pearce and brought before Commissioner Ryals. Their bond was fixed at $200 in each case. The first hearing of the case will be held on Oct. 20.

United States Attorney Akerman, who has been at the Pulaski, returned to his home in Macon last night.

Olsen is already under bond for his appearance to answer the charge against him for kidnapping, in a similar manner, young Joseph Terrell Rucker and John Seage from this port several weeks ago. It will be remembered that the two lads were taken away aboard the British bark Kambira, bound for Santos, Brazil.

8 SHANCHAIED ON ONE VESSEL Moses Smallwood Tells an Amazing Story of Kidnapping of the Laborers from the Docks at Savannah. PUT ON A RUSSIAN BARK AND ALL CRUELLY BEATEN. Discharged Without Pay at Bristol—Smallwood Is Sent Back by the U. S. Consul Alleged Kidnappers Arrested.
When the White Star liner Majestie reached her dock to-day Deputy United States Marshals took from the ship's hospital Moses Smallwood, whose story of shanghaing from the port of Savannah has been seldom paralleled. The United States officials so thoroughly believe the story that they have caused the arrest there of several men said to be in the business of kidnapping both black and white men for service on foreign vessels.

Smallwood was returned to this country by the United States Consul at Bristol, England, to whom the negro first told his story.

"A negro and a white man who runs a sailors' boarding-house in Savannah," he said, "got me drunk the first week in July and rowed me out in the harbor to the Russian bark Alice. The bark was leaking and the pumps had to be manned all the time. All the regular crew had left her, and when I was put on board there were seven other men there, white and black, who had been shanghailed. I fought to get away, but the officers beat me up and I had to stay.

"None of us had ever been on a sailing vessel before. We had done nothing but handle cotton on the levee and about the docks. The officers of the Alice spoke nothing but Russian, and when they would give an order we could not understand them, and then we would get a beating.

"We were out twenty-eight days, and every day each of us got a beating. They shook me down from the ladder several times and my legs are skinned from top to bottom.

"When we got into Bristol we were not allowed to go ashore, but had to unload the cargo of pitch pine. Just as the Alice was ready to sail out of the harbor we were put in a rowboat and told to go where we pleased. We were not paid a cent."

From the numerous whippings and because of their severity, Smallwood was in the Majestic's hospital all the way across the Atlantic. The officers said they had never before heard of such cruelty and barbarity.

The United States officials have arrested at Savannah, Harry Oleson, the keeper of a sailor's boarding-house, and Jake Johnson, a negro. Both are accused of being the kidnappers. Smallwood will be taken to Savannah to testify against them.

SMALLWOOD HERE, TELLS STORY OF HIS TRIP ACROSS.
One of Eight Kidnapped Negroes Gives His Version of the Affair. Moses Smallwood, one of the eight pe
One of Eight Kidnapped Negroes
Gives His Version of the Affair.

Moses Smallwood, one of the eight negroes who were taken to Bristol aboard the bark Alice, for whose kidnapping Harry Olsen and Jake Johnson will have to answer in the United States court, arrived in Savannah on schedule time, as announced in the telegram received by United States Assistant District Attorney W. R. Leaken, which was contained in the Morning News.

This is the story that Smallwood tells:

"The 1st of July I went to a sailors' boarding house in Savannah, run by a white man and a negro. I had not been in the house more than a few hours when a bearded man came in and spoke for a short time in whispers to the white man. As soon as this man went out the boarding house keepers called several of us to the bar and treated. I had taken only a few drinks when I felt drowsy. I lost my senses, and the next thing that I knew I was on a tug that was well out to sea, with seven other negroes. The white man and the bearded man that had talked with him the day before were also on board. They told us that they were taking us out to do some stevedoring. Instead of that we were put on board the Russian bark Alice and thrust below. I fought to get away, and had a fight with the second officer. As he had a belaying pin and I had nothing, I got only a good licking and had to stay.

"Neither myself nor my companions were seamen, and we didn't know one thing from another on board. We had done nothing but hustle cotton bales on board ship before. The bark was leaking, and her regular crew, knowing her condition, had skipped out, along with the rats. We were at the pumps day in and day out, working until our hands were worn to the bone and we would drop on the deck exhausted, to sleep where we fell.

"We were out twenty-eight days, and not a day passed that one or more of us would be knocked the length of the deck because we did not understand our orders. None of the officers could speak anything but Russian. When we got into Bristol we did not get any shore leave, but had to stay aboard and help unload. When the Alice was about to sail we were thrown into a small rowboat and told to go to —. We went ashore, instead. I then went to the Russian consulate to complain of my treatment, and got no satisfaction. Then I applied for aid to the United States consul, who furnished myself and the others shanghaied with transportation home."

COMES TO TESTIFY IN SHANGHAI CASE.
John Gilliard Arrived Yesterday from Delaware. The last of the duo progres John
The last of the five negroes, John Gilliard, who have been brought back to Savannah to testify in the shanghaiing cases in which John Blum and Henry Olsen will figure as defendants, arrived in the city from Philadelphia yesterday, coming to the city from Wilmington, Del., on one of the boats of the Merchants and Miners Transportation Company.

Gilliard's story will be very damaging evidence, he claiming that he was a farmer, and coming to Savannah to sell vegetables, went aboard the Russian bark Alice to deliver some potatoes, and while aboard, the vessel set sail, he being detained aboard and denied the privilege of swimming ashore. He was transported to Bristol, England, only arriving again on American soil last week on the British ship Cymbeline.

Gilliard, upon his arrival here, reported to the United States marshal's office, and was instructed to remain in Savannah until the case comes up in the United States court in January or February, when he will appear to testify against Henry Olsen.
savannah-savannah-1903-09.A17:
OLSEN PUT ON TRIAL
EVIDENCE TAKEN IN THE CASES AGAINST ALLEGED "CRIMPERS."
VICTIMS WERE NOT PUT UP.
LITTLE EVIDENCE THAT THE MEN WERE FORCIBLY EMBARKED.
Of the Eight Negroes Put Aboard the Alice, and of Whom Olsen and Johnson Were Accused of Shanghai, None Were Put on the Witness Stand—All of the Evidence Introduced Went to Show That the Only Objections the Men Offered Was to the Rig of the Ship on Which They Were to Ship—It Was a Bark and They Thought It Was to Be a Schooner.

Harry Olsen and Jack Johnson were arraigned before United States Commissioner Hewlett yesterday afternoon on the charges of shanghaiing, preferred against them some time ago. After the hearing the commissioner reserved his decision.

The witnesses in the cases against Olsen and Johnson were eight negroes, claimed to have been placed on board the tug McCauley some months ago and carried down the river to Sapelo, where the Russian bark Alice was anchored, and were forced to go aboard at the point of a pistol. None of the eight negroes, whose names are Moses Smallwood, John Porter, Joe Easterlin, Jesse Hall, William Jones, James Gillard, Ben Manigault and Benty Washington, were put on the stand, and there was no testimony introduced to show that any of the negroes had been taken aboard the bark against their will, or that they had been carried aboard in a drunken condition.

Capt. Brown's Testimony.

The first witness put on the stand was Capt. John Browne of the tug McCauley. Capt. Browne said that he carried eight negroes down the river to Sapelo and transferred them to the bark Alice. They seemed to be in a perfectly sober condition. The arrangements for the transportation of the negroes was made with Capt. Browne by Capt. Avery, the price paid for their transportation being $20. The money was paid to him by Harry Olsen. Capt. Browne was in the pilot house of the tug going down the river, but did not notice that any of the men were drunk. When they drew alongside the bark some of the men objected to going aboard, as they said they thought they were going to ship on a schooner for New York. Olsen and Johnson got aboard the bark and told the men to come on, that the boat was alright. Capt. Browne said he was bound for Brunswick, and did not want to carry the eight men with him, and he told them to get off. They did so after a short while. There were no threats or intimidation on the part of Olsen, Johnson or any of the officers of the bark, he said.

Heard No Complaints.

Capt. Browne returned from Brunswick a few days later and again tied up by the side of the bark, intending to tow her out to sea, but found that this could not be done until the following day, so he lay alongside the bark all night. During that time he heard no complaints from any of the men on board, though he was in speaking distance. They all seemed to be cheerful, and none of them asked to be brought back to Savannah.

Gus Anderson, who was mate on the McCauley at the time the men were carried down and put on board the Alice, said that he remembered the time the men in question were carried and put on board the Alice. None of them were drunk or drinking, though Olsen had a jug of whisky, which he said he had for his own use. The only objection the men seemed to have to going aboard the Alice was the rig of the vessel. They seemed to be under the impression that they were to board a schooner for New York. He said there were no firearms displayed by any one, nor threats used to get the men to board the bark.

Two negroes were introduced to testify that they had seen Olsen buying clothing for the eight negroes at Kelly's. They said they did not know whether the men were drinking or not.

Obsen's Statement.

Olsen was put on the stand and said that he had received $10 for each man that he had furnished to the captain of the bark, and had paid $20 of this amount to the captain of the tug for transportation, and had furnished the men with oil skin clothing. He said he did not give them whisky or force them in any way to go aboard the tug or to leave the tug and go aboard the bark.

Assistant District Attorney Leaken did not put up any of the eight witnesses, they being the men who were shipped to Bristol, England, and at the conclusion of Olsen's testimony the case was argued before the commissioner by Col. Robert Colding for the defense, and Assistant District Attorney Leaken for the prosecution.

Commissioner Hewlett stated that in view of some technicalities bearing on the case, and the gravity of the decision, which would, in a measure, set a precedent, he would reserve his decision.

OLSEN INDICTED IN SHANGHAI CASES.
United States Grand Jury Finished Its Work.
United States Grand Jury Finished Its Work.

The United States grand jury returned true bills against Harry Olsen yesterday, indicting him upon four separate charges of shanghaiing. Whitty McDonald, a negro, who is charged with assisting Mr. Olsen in deporting the parties who were shanghaied, was also indicted.

The Olsen indictment is the initial case of its kind that has been brought into court in this section, and will probably be the first to go before a jury since the enactment of the shanghai law.

The cases in which Olsen figures as a conspicuous character, are remarkable in many respects. The stories told by the shanghaied men upon their return to Savannah read like fiction. The indictments were returned against Olsen for shanghaiing Joseph Terrell Rucker, John William Seag, Mose Smallwood and Joseph Easterlin, the latter two of whom are negroes and who are only the two of eight who Olsen is alleged to have shanghaied, and who have returned to Savannah. They were shipped to Bristol aboard the Russian bark Alice.

The harrowing details of the experience of the white boys, Joseph Terrell Rucker and John William Seag, their shipment aboard the British bark, Kambira, and their arrival at Santos, Brazil, have summoned the sympathizes of those, who have heard them, and rumors have been afloat to the effect that the prosecution of Olsen and his confederate would not be pushed inasmust as the law prohibiting shanghaiing is a new one. Shanghai or kidnapping, however, mean practically the same thing as peonage, and the important cases now being heard in the United States court, and the fact that the grand jury has indicted Olsen and the McDonald negro, will probably set such rumors at rest.

The cases are in the hands of Assistant United States District Attorney, W. R. Leaken, who has entire charge of them and will push the prosecution vigorously.

Indictments were also returned against Parker White, the charge being robbery of the mails. Other cases of minor importance were also investigated by the grand jury and indictments returned.

Thanked Judge Speer.

The grand jury extended to Judge Speer its thanks for his unusually entertaining charge, and received the following reply from him:

"Your conduct at this term has been an object lesson to the jurors of your country everywhere, and particularly to the jurors of our Southern country. No matter how strong these feelings of race prejudice which dominate all of us more or less, and which are sometimes invoked in public addresses with direct injury to a large class of our humble people, you have demonstrated the fact that you are above considerations of that sort when right and justice are at stake. You have shown yourselves to be humane and just men, true and upright jurors, and most cordially I thank you in behalf of the public. Wishing you long lives and much happiness, you are now discharged for the term."

Graphic Accounts of Voyage to Bristol Told by the Witnesses. Claimed That They Were Cruelly Treated and Severely Whipped. Made to Perform Unaccustomed Tasks, They Said—Found Few of Their Own Color in Bristol. Ragged and Dirty, Their Aspect Frightened People.

In the United States court yesterday Harry Olsen was found guilty of "shanghaling" Mose Smallwood, a negro. United States Attorney's Leaken and Akerman represented the government, and Col. Robert L. Colding looked after the interests of Olsen.

The government made out its case with comparatively little difficulty, all of the witnesses called testifying to the fact that Smallwood had been taken aboard the vessel against his will. Though Olsen denied this charge, the evidence against him, in the minds of the jury, was sufficient to justify a verdict of guilty. Judge Speer reserved sentence until this morning.

The government alleged that Smallwood was one of eight negroes whom Olsen had induced to go aboard a vessel and had then retained him there against his will. The man was shipped to Bristol, England, and because of his lack of seamanship was subjected, it was alleged, to severe punishments and required to do tasks which were physically impossible to a "land lubber."

The story of the "shanghaling was graphically told by the witnesses, and the stories of the treatment they received at sea were vividly brought out.

Whipped Aboard Ship.

Against their will, they testified, Olsen had held them aboard the vessel and not until they were out at sea did they know to what port they were going. Having never had any experience as seamen they could not perform tasks which the ordinary sailor regarded almost as play. For this they were severely whipped, they related.

Time after time they were ordered up the masts, and though unaccustomed to the work, and practically unable to perform the tasks, the officers of the vessel punished them, according to the evidence. The treatment was continued until the negroes were landed at Bristol, and released from the ship.

When they reached Bristol, they said, they were ragged, and dirty, and all spirit had been taken from them by the whippings to which they had been subjected. In the English seaport they found but few of their own color and, friendless and homeless, they could do little for themselves.

**People Were Frightened.**

Their condition was so frightful, they alleged, that the people turned from them in fright and it was impossible to secure any work. No way of returning to this country could be found, until the authorities took the matter in hand.

Through Senator Bard, who interested himself in their behalf, they were transported to their own country again. The attention of the War Department was called to the cases by the Senator, and through that channel their return was effected. The stories of all the witnesses agreed in all the material points.

A receipts for $250, the amount Olsen is alleged to have been given for the negroes, was introduced in evidence.

**Olsen Denied Charges.**

Olsen, in his own behalf, denied the charges that he had put the negroes aboard ship without their consent. He testified that they had been perfectly willing to go with the ship to Bristol, and that no means that were illegitimate were used by him.

Besides securing them the work Olsen stated he had bought clothing for them and aided them materially in other ways.

These statements were denied by the negroes. Once Judge Speer had occasion to remind the witnesses that they were under oath and if they failed to tell the truth they would be punished for perjury.

The Smallwood case was the first of the "shanghai" cases to be tried and the sentence of the court will be awaited with interest. The conviction will probably have the effect of breaking up the practice at this port.

FIVE YEARS FOR SHANGHAIING.
Southern Judge Gives Sailor the Limit and Pleads for Justice to Negroes.
SAVANNAH, Ga., April 7.—Harry Olsen, a sailor runner, who was found guilty yesterday of shanghaiing a number of negroes and sending them to England on the Russian bark Alice, was sentenced to-day to five years in the penitentiary, the maximum term, and to pay a fine of $5,000.

In sentencing the prisoner Judge Emory Speer said that the action of the jury was another exemplification of the truth that the most effective friend of the helpless and unprotected negro is the gentleman of the Southern communities. They know his weakness, he said, but are never slow when he is in the right, or when he has been wronged, to come to his assistance or his defence.

"While this is true," he continued, "it is probably also true that representative Southern people are not aware of the excesses and cruelties to which the lawless and vicious sometimes resort in depriving helpless colored men of their liberties. We cannot have a stable prosperity when any class of citizenship, however humble, can be criminally deprived of liberty without due process of law."

THE SOUTH Is Best Place For the Negro, SAYS BOOKER WASHINGTON. DRAWS LESSON FROM RECENT OCCURRENCES. DISTURBANCE AT VINCENNES. Indiana City Aroused Over Alleged Impudence of a Black Man. VIEWS OF JUSTICE BREWER.
Atlanta, Ga., July 13.—[Special.] Booker T. Washington was given an ovation to-night when, at the celebration of the anniversary of the founding of the Colored Congregational church, he spoke on "The Home, Its Influence In the Settlement of the Race Problem." Gov. Terrell and the Mayor occupied places on the stand.

Washington appealed for harmony between the races, and declared the South the best home for the negro. He said in part: "Let us all learn a lesson from one of the greatest of Southerners, Wade Hampton, of South Carolina, when on his dying bed he uttered the words: 'God bless all of my people, white and black.'

Elevation of the Negro.

"Two recent occurrences emphasize the truth that the negro has strong and wise friends here in the very heart of the South. I refer first to the zeal that some of the members of the white race in my own State of Alabama have shown in bringing to proper punishment those guilty of establishing a poenage system under which members of my race have been the sufferers.

"I refer also to the action of the Georgia Legislature, now in sessilon, in refusing to accede to the unwise and unjust division of the public school fund. Few peoplpe are wise enough to understand the economic value of justice, even when considered from no higher point of view. When compared with the limitations and cruelties inflicted upon the Jews in southern parts of Europe in the present time the future of the black man seems much more encouraging.

Work In the South.

"The time has come here in the South when I believe the very highest type of Southern white men and women are going more and more to take a hand in the elevation of the blacks at their doors. In many sections this work is already in progress, and we hail it as the dawning of a brighter day.

"In conclusion, as I have said, whites and blacks are to reside together in this country permanently, and we should lose no opportunity to cultivate in every manly way the greatest harmony between the races. Whoever, North or South, black or white, stirs up strife needlessly by word or deed is an enemy to both races and to his country."

TROUBLE AVERTED.

Vincennes Negro Accused of Impudence To White Man.

Vincennes, Ind., July 13.—[Special.]—Much excitement was caused in the crowded business section to-night, when Henry Thomas, a negro, was arrested by Sergt. McNell on complaint of Commissioner George Gardner. To avoid the crowd the negro was taken through the City Hall and hustled off to jail. Gardner claims the negro elbowed him and others off the sidewalk, and in answer to a protest the negro jeered and cursed those who remonstrated against his impudence. The negro claims that he intended no harm and that he apologized, which Gardner denies. Thomas came here from Terre Haute to-day. He said he had a wife in St. Louis. Many bold and desperate blacks have managed to stop in Vincennes since the race war at Evansville. Some of the most arrogant of them have hurled insulting and humiliating remarks at white people, and serious trouble may be latent. Police are ordering all strange negroes out of Vincennes.

Colored Walking Delegate Is Roughly Handled.
A negro preacher, playing the role of walking delegate and stirring up strife among the negroes of Lee county, below Americus, has been waited upon by a committee of farmers, given a buggy-trace ovation and advised to get back to his home in Columbus as soon as he could travel. It appears that all through Lee county, white persons have recently been having a good deal of trouble with servants and laborers. Cooks, house girls, wash women and field hands have quit, in many cases without warning, and farmers and others dependent on negro labor have been greatly inconvenienced. In many cases the servants and laborers demanded increased wages before quitting. All this trouble, it is said, resulted from the teachings of this negro preacher, Williams, who advised strikes among the colored help, and white citizens resented his interference by giving him about the severest thrashing one of his kind ever received.
